---
title: "Reading"
subtitle: "Primers and tutorials worth your time"
---

Every entry here was retrieved and checked against **PubMed** — title, journal,
year, authors and DOI. Nothing on this page is a remembered citation. Where a
free full text exists in PubMed Central it is marked **[free]**, because a
curriculum that costs nothing should send you to papers that cost nothing.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Why this page links rather than hosts

We checked the licence of all 94 papers through PubMed. The result is worth
knowing before anyone proposes bundling PDFs with the course:

| | Papers |
|---|---|
| Open licence (Creative Commons) | **7** |
| All rights reserved or unstated, but free to *read* on PubMed Central | **38** |
| No free full text found | **49** |
| Carrying a plain **CC BY** licence | **1** |

: Counts from PubMed and PubMed Central metadata. Treat the open-licence row as a
**floor rather than an exact figure**: two papers whose PDFs we later opened
(van der Graaf, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; Lesko, CC BY-NC-ND) carry Creative Commons
terms that the API had not reported. Neither is BY-SA-compatible, so the
practical conclusion below is unchanged — but the number is a lower bound.

**Free to read is not free to redistribute.** Forty-five of these are readable
at no cost on PubMed Central, and that is a permission to read, not a licence to
copy. Redistributing those PDFs — in this repository, in a course pack, in a
shared folder — would infringe copyright.

Six of the seven openly licensed papers still cannot be folded into this site.
(The strand D additions of August 2026 brought twenty more papers, and the
strand C additions eleven more; none of the thirty-one is openly licensed, so
the open-licence count did not move — a fair illustration of the base rate in
this literature. The three strand C papers counted as free to read carry PubMed
Central identifiers; the specific licence terms of the eleven were **not**
individually checked, so the open-licence row remains a floor.)
This curriculum is **CC BY-SA 4.0**, and BY-SA is incompatible with both **NC**
(non-commercial) and **ND** (no derivatives). We can cite them, describe their
findings, and quote briefly with attribution. We cannot absorb their text or
adapt their figures.

The seventh is the exception, and it is new. Liu's 2017 review of monoclonal
antibody pharmacokinetics is **CC BY 4.0**, which *is* compatible with BY-SA.
Its figures could be adapted into a lesson with attribution. That is one paper
out of ninety-four, which is itself the argument: the default in this literature
is that you may read but not reuse.

So: **link, never host.** Read them through the DOI or your institution's
subscription. If a lesson needs a figure, we draw our own from the underlying
data or the equations.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The pharmacometrics literature has an unusual gift: *CPT: Pharmacometrics &
Systems Pharmacology* runs a standing tutorial series, most of it open access
and much of it with runnable code in the supplements. If you read nothing else,
read the tutorials.
:::

## Start here

| | Why |
|---|---|
| van der Graaf PH. **Book review: *Introduction to Population Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Analysis With Nonlinear Mixed Effects Models* (Owen & Fiedler-Kelly, Wiley 2014).** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2014;3:e153. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/psp.2014.51) · PMID 25531560 · **[free, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0]** | *Read in full — and it is a **two-page book review**, not a primer.* The first pass of this page described it as an orientation to population modelling; that was wrong, and the correction is left visible rather than quietly deleted. What it is good for: an honest, specific assessment of the **book**, which is the actual resource — the first text dedicated to NONMEM, strong on writing an NM-TRAN control stream and reading the output file, and thin on model evaluation, which van der Graaf names as the chapter most needing expansion. Read the review to decide whether to buy the book. For orientation to population PK/PD itself, use Bauer's two NONMEM tutorials below. |
| Lesko LJ. **Perspective on model-informed drug development.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2021;10:1127–1129. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12699) · PMID 34404115 · **[free, CC BY-NC-ND]** | *Read in full.* Three pages, and the best short answer to "where did MIDD come from and why does it feel administrative?" Traces the lineage — ICH E4 (1994), the FDA guidances of 1998, 1999, 2003 and 2018, Sheiner's learn-versus-confirm, Peck on confirmatory evidence — to codification in **PDUFA VI, 2017**. Two ideas worth stealing: adoption differences between companies are organisational (culture, structure, whether pharmacometrics and biostatistics compete) rather than scientific, and **QSP is "technology push" while PBPK is "market pull"**, which explains their differing regulatory reception better than model quality does. Now the backbone of `S0-00` §4. |
| Mehrotra S, Gobburu J. **Communicating to influence drug development and regulatory decisions: a tutorial.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2016;5:163–172. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12073) · PMID 27299706 · **[free]** | The skill that decides whether your analysis changes anything. Pairs with `S0-00` §5. |

## Strand P · Pharmacology

The first pass of this page was thin here: eighteen lessons on pharmacology
resting on three citations. This section is the second pass. It is organised by
what the lessons need rather than by journal, and several entries are included
because they *contradict* something the field teaches casually.

### Receptors, binding and target engagement

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Kenakin T. **Receptor theory.** *Curr Protoc Pharmacol* 2008;Chapter 1:Unit 1.2. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471141755.ph0102s41) · PMID 22294216 | Classical receptor theory and the operational model, by the person who wrote the textbook. Background for `P-04` and `P-05`. |
| Kenakin T. **Biased agonism.** *F1000 Biol Rep* 2009;1:87. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3410/B1-87) · PMID 20948603 · **[free, CC BY-NC 3.0]** | *Read in full.* Dismantles the receptor-as-switch picture: the minimal unit of control is the agonist–receptor complex, not the receptor, so two agonists can have their relative potencies **reverse** between two readouts. Efficacy is "pluridimensional" — propranolol is an antagonist and inverse agonist at G-protein-mediated effects and an *activator* of ERK. The modelling consequence, now in `P-03`: your choice of biomarker decides which effect you are measuring. |
| Dua P, Hawkins E, van der Graaf PH. **A tutorial on target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) models.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2015;4:324–337. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.41) · PMID 26225261 · **[free, CC BY-NC 4.0]** | *Read in full.* Starts exactly where `P-04` stops — with the Langmuir isotherm and the point at which "drug is in vast excess" fails. Then builds the model ladder: full TMDD, quasi-equilibrium, quasi-steady-state, Michaelis–Menten, and **states the conditions under which each approximation holds**, which is the part you cannot reconstruct yourself. Two corrections it supplies to common belief: TMDD is not a biologics-only phenomenon (Levy's first description was warfarin), and TMDD does not by itself imply nonlinear pharmacokinetics. Berkeley Madonna code in the supplement. |
| Burvenich IJG, Parakh S, Parslow AC, et al. **Receptor occupancy imaging studies in oncology drug development.** *AAPS J* 2018;20:43. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1208/s12248-018-0203-z) · PMID 29520671 | Occupancy stops being a theoretical quantity and becomes a measured one. PET/SPECT competition studies relate plasma concentration directly to fractional occupancy in tissue, which is the only way to answer "does the dose saturate the target?" without inferring it from effect. The empirical companion to `P-04`'s Langmuir arithmetic, and the top of `P-15`'s biomarker hierarchy. |

### Transporters

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Giacomini KM, Huang S-M, Tweedie DJ, et al. **Membrane transporters in drug development.** *Nat Rev Drug Discov* 2010;9:215–236. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd3028) · PMID 20190787 · **[free]** | The International Transporter Consortium's founding white paper, and the document that turned transporters from a research topic into a regulatory expectation. Decision trees for which transporters to study and when. Essential background for `P-03`, where transporters appear as both drug target and obstacle. |
| Galetin A, Brouwer KLR, Tweedie D, et al. **Membrane transporters in drug development and as determinants of precision medicine.** *Nat Rev Drug Discov* 2024;23:255–280. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41573-023-00877-1) · PMID 38267543 · **[free]** | The ITC's fourteen-years-later update. Read after Giacomini, not instead of it: the value is in what changed. |

### Absorption and the fate of an oral dose

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Wu C-Y, Benet LZ. **Predicting drug disposition via application of BCS: transport/absorption/elimination interplay and development of a biopharmaceutics drug disposition classification system.** *Pharm Res* 2005;22:11–23. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11095-004-9004-4) · PMID 15771225 | The BDDCS paper. Reclassifies drugs by *elimination route* rather than permeability alone, and in doing so predicts which compounds will show transporter effects, food effects and drug–drug interactions. Four classes that let you guess a compound's problems before you measure them — the single highest-yield mental model in `P-06`. |
| Deng J, Zhu X, Chen Z, et al. **A review of food-drug interactions on oral drug absorption.** *Drugs* 2017;77:1833–1855. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40265-017-0832-z) · PMID 29076109 | Food effect for 229 drugs, analysed by BDDCS class — the empirical test of the paper above. Turns "take with food" from a label instruction into a mechanism. `P-06`. |

### Distribution and protein binding

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Smith DA, Di L, Kerns EH. **The effect of plasma protein binding on in vivo efficacy: misconceptions in drug discovery.** *Nat Rev Drug Discov* 2010;9:929–939. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd3287) · PMID 21119731 | Free *concentration* governs efficacy; free *fraction* is routinely mistaken for it, and compounds are prioritised on the wrong quantity. Underpins the free-versus-total rule in `S0-02` and `P-08`. |
| Schulz JA, Stresser DM, Kalvass JC. **Plasma protein-mediated uptake and contradictions to the free drug hypothesis: a critical review.** *Drug Metab Rev* 2023;55:205–238. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2023.2195133) · PMID 36971325 | Where the free drug hypothesis breaks: hepatic uptake in which observed unbound intrinsic clearance exceeds prediction. Notably, several candidate mechanisms for the effect remain *consistent* with the free drug hypothesis — the review does not simply overturn it. `P-08`, `P-11`. |
| Nation RL, Theuretzbacher U, Tsuji BT. **Concentration-dependent plasma protein binding: expect the unexpected.** *Eur J Pharm Sci* 2018;122:341–346. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejps.2018.07.004) · PMID 30026170 | Saturable binding raising free fraction with concentration is textbook. This catalogues the drugs that do the *opposite* — free fraction **falls** as concentration rises. A short paper whose whole function is to break the assumption that f~u~ is a constant you can look up. `P-08` failure mode. |
| Ulldemolins M, Roberts JA, Rello J, et al. **The effects of hypoalbuminaemia on optimizing antibacterial dosing in critically ill patients.** *Clin Pharmacokinet* 2011;50:99–110. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2165/11539220-000000000-00000) · PMID 21142293 | What happens when f~u~ changes in a real population: 40–50% of ICU patients are hypoalbuminaemic, and ceftriaxone's V~d~ and CL roughly double. The worked clinical consequence of the two entries above. |

### Clearance, metabolism and the liver

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Mehvar R. **Clearance concepts: fundamentals and application to pharmacokinetic behavior of drugs.** *J Pharm Pharm Sci* 2018;21:88s–102s. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.18433/jpps29896) · PMID 30041730 | The clearest single treatment of extraction ratio, organ blood flow and intrinsic clearance, with the well-stirred and parallel-tube models set side by side and their differing predictions worked numerically. If you read one thing before `P-11`, read this. |
| Benet LZ, Sodhi JK. **Can in vitro–in vivo extrapolation be successful? Recognizing the incorrect clearance assumptions.** *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 2022;111:1022–1035. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2482) · PMID 34731496 · **[free]** | Read this *against* Mehvar, deliberately. Benet and Sodhi argue that the well-stirred equation taught in every PK course "has no validity", that all published clearances are arterial clearances, and that IVIVE has no theoretical basis. **This is a contested position, not settled fact** — it is here because a curriculum that only ever shows you the consensus teaches you to trust equations you have never seen attacked. `P-11`'s designated controversy. |
| Pang KS, Durk MR. **Physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modeling for absorption, transport, metabolism and excretion.** *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 2010;37:591–615. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10928-010-9185-x) · PMID 21153869 | The lineage from Rowland's 1973 liver model to modern PBPK, including why the Rodgers–Rowland tissue-partition work mattered so much. The bridge from `P-11` to strand `S3`. |
| Tompkins LM, Wallace AD. **Mechanisms of cytochrome P450 induction.** *J Biochem Mol Toxicol* 2007;21:176–181. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/jbt.20180) · PMID 17936931 | Induction as transcription: PXR, CAR and AhR, and why CYP3A4, 2B6 and 1A1 respond to different signals. Short. Explains why an induction interaction takes days to appear and days to wash out, which inhibition does not. `P-09`. |

### The kidney

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Verbeeck RK, Musuamba FT. **Pharmacokinetics and dosage adjustment in patients with renal dysfunction.** *Eur J Clin Pharmacol* 2009;65:757–773. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00228-009-0678-8) · PMID 19543887 | Renal impairment does more than slow renal excretion: it lowers protein binding and suppresses drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters. The standard reference for `P-10`, and the reason dose adjustment cannot be read off GFR alone. |
| Pradhan S, Duffull SB, Walker RJ, Wright DFB. **The intact nephron hypothesis as a model for renal drug handling.** *Eur J Clin Pharmacol* 2019;75:147–156. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00228-018-2572-8) · PMID 30298363 | Every time you put creatinine clearance on CL as a linear covariate, you are assuming the intact nephron hypothesis. This systematic review found **24 of 30 studies did not support it**, and the studies that did tended to use weaker methods. Read it before you write `CL = θ · (CRCL/100)^θ2` again. `P-10` and `S2`. |
| Wang X, Mu J, Ma K, Ma Y. **Challenges of serum creatinine level in GFR assessment and drug dosing decisions in kidney injury.** *Adv Pharm Bull* 2024;14:745–758. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.34172/apb.42345) · PMID 40190670 · **[free]** | Serum creatinine is itself filtered, secreted, reabsorbed and eliminated extra-renally, and is perturbed by muscle mass, trauma, HIV and drug–creatinine interactions. So the covariate is noisy in ways that are not random. Directly relevant to `CASE-SM`, where `CRCL` is a **decoy** covariate with no true effect. |

### Physiology and special populations

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Anderson BJ, Holford NHG. **Mechanistic basis of using body size and maturation to predict clearance in humans.** *Drug Metab Pharmacokinet* 2009;24:25–36. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2133/dmpk.24.25) · PMID 19252334 | The argument for allometric scaling and for maturation functions in children. Underpins `S0-02` and `P-12`. |
| Rhodin MM, Anderson BJ, Peters AM, et al. **Human renal function maturation: a quantitative description using weight and postmenstrual age.** *Pediatr Nephrol* 2009;24:67–76. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00467-008-0997-5) · PMID 18846389 | GFR from premature neonate to adult in one model. The worked example of why size alone fails in paediatrics. |
| Abduljalil K, Pan X, Pansari A, Jamei M, Johnson TN. **A preterm physiologically based pharmacokinetic model. Part I: physiological parameters and model building.** *Clin Pharmacokinet* 2020;59:485–500. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40262-019-00825-6) · PMID 31583613 | Where the numbers come from. Organ sizes as functions of body weight, protein binding as a function of age, ontogeny functions for CYP1A2, 3A4 and 2C9 — collated because they exist in no single source. Also states plainly which values are thin (tissue composition). `P-12`. |

### Biologics

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Lobo ED, Hansen RJ, Balthasar JP. **Antibody pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.** *J Pharm Sci* 2004;93:2645–2668. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/jps.20178) · PMID 15389672 | The paper that set out why antibodies behave unlike small molecules: saturable target binding, FcRn-dependent concentration-dependent elimination, and immunogenicity altering a drug's own kinetics. Background for `P-01`'s modality survey and for `CASE-MAB`. |
| Keizer RJ, Huitema ADR, Schellens JHM, Beijnen JH. **Clinical pharmacokinetics of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies.** *Clin Pharmacokinet* 2010;49:493–507. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2165/11531280-000000000-00000) · PMID 20608753 | The clinical view: low volumes of distribution, half-lives up to four weeks, body size relationships that are statistically real and clinically minor, and the near-absence of metabolic drug–drug interactions. |
| Liu L. **Pharmacokinetics of monoclonal antibodies and Fc-fusion proteins.** *Protein Cell* 2017;9:15–32. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13238-017-0408-4) · PMID 28421387 · **[free, CC BY 4.0]** | The most current of the three, and the only paper on this entire page under a plain **CC BY** licence — which means, uniquely, that its figures could be adapted into this site with attribution. Covers Fc engineering for half-life, charge and glycosylation effects, subcutaneous absorption via lymphatics, and human PK prediction from cynomolgus data. |

### Cell and gene therapy kinetics

Listed as a gap in the first pass. `CASE-CELL` will need these.

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Stein AM, Grupp SA, Levine JE, et al. **Tisagenlecleucel model-based cellular kinetic analysis of chimeric antigen receptor-T cells.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2019;8:285–295. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12388) · PMID 30848084 · **[free]** | The first mixed-effects model of a CAR-T product. Doubling time 0.78 days, initial decline half-life 4.3 days, terminal half-life 220 days — a "drug" whose kinetics are expansion and contraction, not absorption and elimination. |
| Liu C, Ayyar VS, Zheng X, et al. **Model-based cellular kinetic analysis of chimeric antigen receptor-T cells in humans.** *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 2021;109:716–727. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2040) · PMID 33002189 · **[free]** | 217 patients across seven trials. Responders show higher proliferation and slower contraction; haematologic tumours support more expansion than solid ones; and **dose is only weakly related to exposure or response** — which is roughly the opposite of the small-molecule intuition. |
| Chaudhury A, Zhu X, Chu L, et al. **Chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapies: a review of cellular kinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling approaches.** *J Clin Pharmacol* 2020;60(S1):S147–S159. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcph.1691) · PMID 33205434 | A taxonomy of the model structures, and where to extend them: target binding, tumour distribution, cytokine release syndrome, immunophenotype differentiation. Read after the two above. |

## Strand D · Disease areas — D1 pancreatic cancer

Twenty references gathered *before* the lessons that will use them, which is the
opposite of how strand `P` was built. All verified through PubMed; all
annotations rest on abstracts. See [Strand D](diseases.qmd) for the lesson
outline these support.

### Disease biology

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Ying H, Kimmelman AC, Bardeesy N, Kalluri R, Maitra A, DePinho RA. **Genetics and biology of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.** *Genes Dev* 2025;39:36–63. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.351863.124) · PMID 39510840 · **[free]** | The current synthesis: genomic landscape, the cellular composition of the microenvironment from single-cell work, and metabolic cross-talk between cancer and stromal cells. Written at the point KRAS-targeted therapy became real, so it is unusually clear about what changed. `D1-02`, `D1-05`. |
| Wood LD, Canto MI, Jaffee EM, Simeone DM. **Pancreatic cancer: pathogenesis, screening, diagnosis, and treatment.** *Gastroenterology* 2022;163:386–402. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.03.056) · PMID 35398344 · **[free]** | Broadest single entry point — molecular alterations, microenvironment, population risk, screening, and how treatment changes with stage. The orientation reference for `D1-01`. |
| Vincent A, Herman J, Schulick R, Hruban RH, Goggins M. **Pancreatic cancer.** *Lancet* 2011;378:607–620. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)62307-0) · PMID 21620466 · **[free]** | Older, and included for one reason: it states plainly that 80–85% of patients present with advanced unresectable disease. That single number explains the shape of every trial population you will model. |
| Storz P. **Acinar cell plasticity and development of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.** *Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol* 2017;14:296–304. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrgastro.2017.12) · PMID 28270694 · **[free]** | Acinar-to-ductal metaplasia as the initiating step. Matters for `D1-03` because it determines what the preclinical models actually model. |
| McGuigan A, Kelly P, Turkington RC, et al. **Pancreatic cancer: a review of clinical diagnosis, epidemiology, treatment and outcomes.** *World J Gastroenterol* 2018;24:4846–4861. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3748/wjg.v24.i43.4846) · PMID 30487695 · **[free]** | Epidemiology and outcomes, with five-year survival of 2–9% — last among all cancer sites. `D1-01`. |
| Bailey P, Chang DK, Nones K, et al. **Genomic analyses identify molecular subtypes of pancreatic cancer.** *Nature* 2016;531:47–52. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16965) · PMID 26909576 | 456 tumours; 32 recurrently mutated genes aggregating into 10 pathways; four expression subtypes — squamous, pancreatic progenitor, immunogenic, ADEX — with squamous carrying a poor prognosis. `D1-04` has to decide whether any of this belongs in a covariate model. |

### The stroma, and the experiment that tested it

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Hosein AN, Brekken RA, Maitra A. **Pancreatic cancer stroma: an update on therapeutic targeting strategies.** *Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol* 2020;17:487–505. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41575-020-0300-1) · PMID 32393771 · **[free]** | The three stromal compartments — extracellular matrix, vasculature, cancer-associated fibroblasts — and a decade of attempts to target each. States the mechanism `D1-05` and `D1-06` rest on: the matrix functions as a barrier to drug delivery. |
| Wang W-Q, Liu L, Xu J-Z, Yu X-J. **Reflections on depletion of tumor stroma in pancreatic cancer.** *Biochim Biophys Acta Rev Cancer* 2019;1871:267–272. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbcan.2019.01.007) · PMID 30738097 | The counter-argument, and the reason `D1-07` is not a simple story: the stroma also *inhibits* metastasis, so depleting it is double-edged. A mechanism can be real and targeting it can still make things worse. |
| Dimou A, Syrigos KN, Saif MW. **Overcoming the stromal barrier: technologies to optimize drug delivery in pancreatic cancer.** *Ther Adv Med Oncol* 2012;4:271–279. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/1758834012446008) · PMID 22942909 · **[free]** | The delivery-optimisation framing as it stood before the phase 3 results came in. Useful as a record of what the field believed. |
| Hingorani SR, Zheng L, Bullock AJ, et al. **HALO 202: randomized phase II study of PEGPH20 plus nab-paclitaxel/gemcitabine.** *J Clin Oncol* 2018;36:359–366. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2017.74.9564) · PMID 29232172 | The encouraging phase 2. PFS hazard ratio 0.73 overall, **0.51 in hyaluronan-high tumours** — a biomarker-selected signal that justified a phase 3. |
| Van Cutsem E, Tempero MA, Sigal D, et al. **Randomized phase III trial of pegvorhyaluronidase alfa with nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine for hyaluronan-high metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma.** *J Clin Oncol* 2020;38:3185–3194. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.20.00590) · PMID 32706635 · **[free]** | **The lesson.** 492 biomarker-selected patients. Objective response rate rose, 47% versus 36%. Median overall survival: **11.2 versus 11.5 months, hazard ratio 1.00**. The mechanism was real, the biomarker enriched the population, the response endpoint moved — and survival did not. `D1-07` is built entirely on the distance between those results. |

### Treatment, and what any new model must beat

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Conroy T, Desseigne F, Ychou M, et al. **FOLFIRINOX versus gemcitabine for metastatic pancreatic cancer.** *N Engl J Med* 2011;364:1817–1825. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1011923) · PMID 21561347 | Median OS 11.1 versus 6.8 months, HR 0.57, with substantially more toxicity — 5.4% febrile neutropenia. The efficacy–tolerability trade-off that dose-optimisation work in this disease inherits. |
| Goldstein D, El-Maraghi RH, Hammel P, et al. **nab-Paclitaxel plus gemcitabine for metastatic pancreatic cancer: long-term survival from a phase III trial.** *J Natl Cancer Inst* 2015;107:dju413. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/jnci/dju413) · PMID 25638248 | MPACT long-term follow-up: OS 8.7 versus 6.6 months, HR 0.72. Also reports baseline CA19-9 and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio as prognostic, which is where `D1-10` starts. |
| Wang-Gillam A, Hubner RA, Siveke JT, et al. **NAPOLI-1 phase 3 study of liposomal irinotecan: final overall survival analysis.** *Eur J Cancer* 2019;108:78–87. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.007) · PMID 30654298 | Second-line, post-gemcitabine: OS 6.2 versus 4.2 months, HR 0.75. Also identifies the baseline characteristics associated with surviving a year. |
| Ohhashi S, Ohuchida K, Mizumoto K, et al. **Down-regulation of deoxycytidine kinase enhances acquired resistance to gemcitabine in pancreatic cancer.** *Anticancer Res* 2008;28:2205–2212. · PMID 18751396 | Mechanistic, and the basis for `D1-09`: gemcitabine requires intracellular phosphorylation by deoxycytidine kinase, so resistance can arise entirely downstream of plasma exposure. **No DOI is registered for this article** — cite by PMID. |
| Humphris JL, Chang DK, Johns AL, et al. **The prognostic and predictive value of serum CA19.9 in pancreatic cancer.** *Ann Oncol* 2012;23:1713–1722. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdr561) · PMID 22241899 · **[free]** | CA19-9 in 260 resected patients, with the awkward detail `D1-10` must handle: the marker is informative only in patients who express it, and the paper defines that subgroup explicitly. |

### The modelling framework

Not PDAC-specific, and the quantitative backbone of `D1-11`.

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Claret L, Girard P, Hoff PM, et al. **Model-based prediction of phase III overall survival in colorectal cancer on the basis of phase II tumor dynamics.** *J Clin Oncol* 2009;27:4103–4108. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2008.21.0807) · PMID 19636014 | The paper that established the approach: a longitudinal tumour growth inhibition model plus a parametric survival model, used to predict a phase 3 outcome from phase 2 data. Predicted median survival 431 days against 401 observed. |
| Bruno R, Mercier F, Claret L. **Evaluation of tumor size response metrics to predict survival in oncology clinical trials.** *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 2014;95:386–393. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/clpt.2014.4) · PMID 24419563 | The review of *which* tumour-size metric predicts survival, and an honest account of why the approach is not yet routine despite being available for a decade. |
| Claret L, Mercier F, Houk BE, Milligan PA, Bruno R. **Modeling and simulations relating overall survival to tumor growth inhibition in renal cell carcinoma patients.** *Cancer Chemother Pharmacol* 2015;76:567–573. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00280-015-2820-x) · PMID 26198314 | 2,552 patients across ten studies. Time to tumour growth was the best predictor of survival, but week-8 early tumour shrinkage performed well enough to be preferred for its clinical usability — a real methodological trade-off, stated. |
| Claret L, Zheng J, Mercier F, et al. **Model-based prediction of progression-free survival using week 8 tumor size change from baseline.** *Cancer Chemother Pharmacol* 2016;78:605–610. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00280-016-3116-5) · PMID 27468922 | Extends the framework to progression-free survival with external validation, and simulates the hazard ratio a new agent would need to achieve. |

### The therapeutic landscape, August 2026

Added 30 August 2026, after the first RAS inhibitor was approved in this disease.
These ten support the *therapeutic landscape* section of
[Strand D](diseases.qmd) and rewrite what `D1-08` and `D1-11` have to cover.

| | Why |
|---|---|
| O'Reilly EM, Wainberg ZA, Hendifar AE, et al. **Daraxonrasib in previously treated metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.** *N Engl J Med* 2026;395:325–337. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2605555) · PMID 42223072 | RASolute 302. 500 patients, 91.8% KRAS G12. Median OS **13.2 vs 6.6 months, HR 0.40**; discontinuation for treatment-related events **1.2% vs 11.2%**. The second number is the one to teach: the targeted agent was both more effective and nine times less likely to be stopped. `D1-08`. |
| Aronchik I, et al. **Molecular determinants of response and resistance to daraxonrasib in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.** *Nat Med* 2026;32:2865–2877. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04537-w) · PMID 42581230 | Paired ctDNA, 44 patients. Mutant KRAS **amplification** in 36%; **zero** acquired secondary KRAS mutations. Resistance by making more target, not by changing its shape — an occupancy problem, which is why strand `P` transfers directly. |
| Wainberg ZA, Melisi D, Macarulla T, et al. **NALIRIFOX versus nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine in treatment-naive metastatic PDAC.** *Lancet* 2023;402:1272–1281. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(23)01366-1) · PMID 37708904 | NAPOLI 3. The current first-line comparator: 11.1 vs 9.2 months, HR 0.83, with grade ≥3 events of 87% vs 86%. A 1.9-month gain at identical toxicity is the honest baseline any new agent is measured against. |
| Golan T, Hammel P, Reni M, et al. **Maintenance olaparib for germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic cancer.** *N Engl J Med* 2019;381:317–327. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1903387) · PMID 31157963 · **[free]** | POLO. PFS 7.4 vs 3.8 months (HR 0.53) and no OS difference at interim. Read it for the screening ratio — **3,315 screened to randomise 154** — which is the practical ceiling on allele-specific strategies here. |
| Nicolle R, Bachet JB, Harlé A, et al. **Prediction of adjuvant gemcitabine sensitivity using the GemPred RNA signature.** *J Clin Oncol* 2023;42:1067–1076. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.22.02668) · PMID 37963313 · **[free]** | Ancillary to PRODIGE 24. 25.5% of resected patients did as well on gemcitabine as on mFOLFIRINOX, with grade ≥3 events of 40% vs 76%. A biomarker that would de-escalate rather than escalate, which is rare and worth a lesson. |
| Weller C, Burnett GL, Jiang L, et al. **A neomorphic protein interface catalyzes covalent inhibition of RAS aspartic acid in tumors.** *Science* 2025;389:eads0239. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ads0239) · PMID 40705880 | How zoldonrasib (RMC-9805) targets G12D: recruiting cyclophilin A to build a neomorphic interface that catalytically accelerates covalent reaction with a poor nucleophile. Medicinal chemistry worth reading even if you never model it. |
| Pillozzi S, Giommoni E, Petroni G, et al. **The KRAS targeting revolution in metastatic pancreatic cancer.** *J Hematol Oncol* 2026;19(1). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13045-026-01834-2) · PMID 42571010 · **[free]** | Short correspondence surveying the allele-specific pipeline as presented at ASCO 2026. The fastest orientation to what is behind daraxonrasib. |
| Khan HY, Al Hallak MN, Aboukameel A, et al. **XPO1 inhibition enhances the efficacy and durability of RAS-targeted therapy in KRAS-G12D PDAC.** *Cancer Lett* 2026;218804. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218804) · PMID 42667948 | **Preclinical only.** Listed because combination strategies against adaptive resistance are where this field goes next, and because the distance between an organoid result and a phase 3 is itself a teaching point. |
| Parganiha M, Rathored J, Sai Painkra D. **mRNA vaccines in oncology: personalized cancer immunization and neoantigen targeting.** *Mol Cell Oncol* 2026;13(1):2652613. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/23723556.2026.2652613) · PMID 41971684 · **[free]** | Reports autogene cevumeran in resected PDAC: 8 of 16 immune responders, recurrence not reached vs 13.4 months. Useful **as a caution** — the hazard ratio comes from an 8-patient subgroup defined by response to the intervention. |
| Ye L, Zhao G, Ma J, et al. **Personalized cancer vaccines: bridging immune-oncology and precision medicine.** *Signal Transduct Target Ther* 2026;11(1). [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41392-026-02769-3) · PMID 42481451 · **[free]** | The broader review around that result, covering platforms, delivery and why clinical translation has been so slow. |

## Strand C · Approved drugs — clinical pharmacology from the regulatory record

Eleven papers gathered before the lessons, as with strand `D`. All verified
through PubMed; all annotations rest on abstracts. See
[Strand C](drugs.qmd) for the outline they support, and for the twelve FDA
approval packages — public-domain documents, cited from
[Resources](resources.qmd) rather than from here.

### A model in place of a trial

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Lala M, Li TR, de Alwis DP, et al. **A six-weekly dosing schedule for pembrolizumab in patients with cancer based on evaluation using modelling and simulation.** *Eur J Cancer* 2020;131:68–75. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.02.016) · PMID 32305010 | The central document of `C-02`. A population model on 2,993 subjects from five trials, used to bridge 400 mg Q6W to the established 200 mg Q3W on exposure alone: average concentration about 1% higher, peak concentration roughly 65% below the highest dose ever given clinically. Read it for the structure of the argument, not the result. |
| Lala M, Li TR, de Alwis DP, et al. **Corrigendum.** *Eur J Cancer* 2021;144:400. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.12.006) · PMID 33414065 | Listed separately and deliberately. `C-02` teaches close reading of a regulatory argument; citing the paper without its correction would undercut the lesson. |
| Zhao Y, Tsujimoto A, Ide T, et al. **Model-based population pharmacokinetic and exposure response analyses for safety and efficacy of nivolumab as adjuvant treatment in subjects with resected oesophageal or gastroesophageal junction cancer.** *Br J Clin Pharmacol* 2024;90:2920–2930. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16188) · PMID 39054780 | PopPK on 1,493 subjects; exposure–response on 756 from CheckMate 577. Hazard ratios at the 5th and 95th exposure percentiles were similar for both disease-free survival and grade ≥2 immune-mediated events. `C-03` is about what a flat relationship licenses — and what it quietly does not. |

### Doses that were argued over

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Ratain MJ, Tannock IF, Lichter AS. **Dose optimization of sotorasib: is the US Food and Drug Administration sending a message?** *J Clin Oncol* 2021;39:3423–3426. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.21.01371) · PMID 34543056 | Three pages, and the sharpest regulatory argument on this page. The origin text for `C-04` and for the Project Optimus framing that runs through the strand. |
| Hanley MJ, Diderichsen P, Rich B, et al. **Response-based dosing for ponatinib: model-based analyses of the dose-ranging OPTIC study.** *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 2023;114:413–422. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2956) · PMID 37219378 | A four-state discrete-time Markov model for molecular response, time-to-event models for harm. A 15 mg dose increase gave an odds ratio of 2.05 (95% CI 1.53–2.89) for one response transition and a hazard ratio of 2.05 (95% CI 1.43–2.93) for arterial occlusive events. `C-05` exists because those two numbers are the same. |

| | Why |
|---|---|

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacl.2023.04.010) · PMID 37164838 | Single subcutaneous dose, elimination half-life 6.5 hours, LDL-C still down 49.6% (100 mg) and 58.3% (300 mg) at day 90. The cleanest published statement of the PK/PD disconnect `C-08` is built on. |
| Barkas F, Ray K. **An update on inclisiran for the treatment of elevated LDL cholesterol.** *Expert Opin Pharmacother* 2024;25:349–358. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/14656566.2024.2337253) · PMID 38549399 | Places inclisiran's kinetics against the PCSK9 antibodies, which is the comparison that makes the disconnect legible rather than merely odd. |

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/cts.13717) · PMID 38266057 · **[free]** | 1.5 mg/kg weekly reached through step-up doses of 0.06 and 0.3 mg/kg, selected on exposure–response for efficacy and safety together. `C-09`: the dose is a schedule, because the toxicity tracks the first exposure rather than the steady-state one. |
| Brendel K, Bekaii-Saab T, Boland PM, et al. **Population pharmacokinetics of liposomal irinotecan in patients with cancer and exposure-safety analyses in patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2021;10:1550–1563. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12725) · PMID 34750990 · **[free]** | 440 patients, seven studies, exposure–safety in mPDAC from NAPOLI-1. Total irinotecan clearance 0.107 L/h against SN-38 clearance 118 L/h; UGT1A1\*28 7/7 homozygosity had **no** significant effect on SN-38 clearance. Shared between `C-11` and `D1-08`, and worth reading for the negative covariate result. |

## Strand S0 · Foundations

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Yates JWT, Jones RDO, Walker M, Cheung SYA. **Structural identifiability and indistinguishability of compartmental models.** *Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol* 2009;5:295–302. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1517/17425250902773426) · PMID 19331592 | The formal basis for `S0-01` §5. Distinguishes structural non-identifiability from model *indistinguishability* — two structures that no amount of data of that type can separate — and notes that the problem is usually only noticed when estimation misbehaves, though its implications for inference apply regardless. |
| Smith DA, Di L, Kerns EH. **The effect of plasma protein binding on in vivo efficacy: misconceptions in drug discovery.** *Nat Rev Drug Discov* 2010;9:929–939. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd3287) · PMID 21119731 | Free *concentration* governs efficacy; free *fraction* is routinely mistaken for it, and compounds are prioritised on the wrong quantity. Underpins the free-versus-total rule in `S0-02`. |
| Beal SL. **Ways to fit a PK model with some data below the quantification limit.** *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 2001;28:481–504. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1012299115260) · PMID 11768292 | The original M1–M7 paper. `S0-03` tells you to flag BLQ and not impute; this is why. |
| Keizer RJ, Karlsson MO, Hooker A. **Modeling and simulation workbench for NONMEM: tutorial on Pirana, PsN, and Xpose.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2013;2:e50. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/psp.2013.24) · PMID 23836189 · **[free, CC BY-NC-ND 3.0]** | *Read in full.* Nominally a software tutorial; in practice the most quotable source on **which diagnostic to trust when**. Supplies the ~5% ε-shrinkage threshold above which \|IWRES\| vs IPRED stops being informative, the sequencing rule (residual-based diagnostics early, simulation-based late), VPC binning guidance (no more bins than observations per individual), the insistence on uncertainty bands rather than bare percentile lines, and bootstrap sample counts (~100 for means, 1,000+ for tail percentiles). Much of `S0-06` now rests on it. |

The remaining twenty-five have no free full text on PubMed Central and need a
subscription. They cluster in the same places: the *Nature Reviews* and
*Clinical Pharmacokinetics* review literature, and the older primary papers.
Among them are Beal on BLQ, Kenakin's *Receptor theory*, Wu & Benet on BDDCS,
Mehvar on clearance concepts, Verbeeck & Musuamba on renal dosing, Pradhan et
al. on the intact nephron hypothesis, and Lobo et al. on antibody PK.

Routes to those, in order of ease: your institution's subscription; an
interlibrary loan; or emailing the corresponding author, which in this field is
normal and usually answered within a day. A handful are also open on their
publisher's own site without a PubMed Central deposit — worth one click on the
DOI before assuming a paywall.

Keep what you download in `reading/papers/`. That directory is gitignored, so
your personal library sits beside the project and never enters the repository.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Where the line falls, concretely. **Fine:** downloading these to read, annotate,
and cite. **Not fine:** committing the PDFs here, putting them in a shared drive
for a cohort, or bundling them as a course pack. If you later teach from this
material, course readings go through your library's reserves system, which
exists precisely to license that use.
:::

## What the one-line notes rest on

Honest provenance, because it varies by entry.

We attempted to retrieve full texts through the PubMed Central API. **Full text
came back only for the openly licensed papers.** For the rest — including the
twenty-one that are free to read in a browser — the API returns the abstract and
an empty body, which tracks the licence status exactly: readable on the PMC
website is not the same as available for programmatic retrieval.

So:

| Entry | The note rests on |
|---|---|
| Dua on TMDD, Keizer on the NONMEM workbench, Kenakin on biased agonism, van der Graaf's book review, Lesko on MIDD | The full text, read |
| The other CC-licensed papers | Retrievable, not yet read |
| The remaining 64 | Title, journal, abstract, and subject knowledge |

**Reading two of them changed two entries, and one of those was an error.** The
van der Graaf item was described here as an orientation to population modelling.
It is a **two-page book review**. That annotation had been written from the title
and the journal, which is exactly the failure mode this section exists to warn
about; the entry now says what the paper is, and the correction is left visible.
The Lesko entry survived contact with its full text and got substantially richer.
One correction and one enrichment out of two papers is not a reassuring hit
rate.

Entries in the third group are a starting map, not a substitute for reading the
paper — and several of them are ones the lessons lean on hardest (Beal on BLQ,
Savic & Karlsson on shrinkage, Anderson & Holford on allometry). Those
annotations describe what the papers are *for*, from their abstracts and their
place in the field, not a close reading.

**The whole of the strand `P` second pass, and all twenty strand `D` entries,
are in that third group.** Those entries were verified against PubMed for title,
journal, year, authors and DOI, and annotated from their abstracts. Where an annotation states
a specific number — 24 of 30 studies, 40–50% of ICU patients, a 0.78-day
doubling time — that number is quoted from the paper's own abstract, not
computed by us and not checked against its results section.

If a note mischaracterises a paper, that is a bug: open an issue and it gets
fixed.

## How to read a tutorial paper

Do not read it like a review. These have supplements with code, and the code is
the point.

1. Read the abstract and skip to the **worked example**.
2. Download the supplement and **run it before understanding it**. Getting the
   authors' output on your machine is worth more than a careful first read.
3. **Break it** — change a parameter, remove a term, see what the diagnostics do.
   This is `S0-01`'s failure-mode habit applied to somebody else's model.
4. Only then read the theory, with a concrete thing in front of you.

## What is missing here

Honest gaps in this list, which will fill as the strands are written:

- **No textbooks.** Rowland & Tozer, Gabrielsson & Weiner and Rang & Dale are
  each worth owning; none is on PubMed, so none is on this page.
- **No software, courses, datasets or reference databases.** By design — those
  are not papers. They are on the [Resources](resources.qmd) page, which is
  generated from a validated CSV in this repository.
- ~~**No regulatory guidances.**~~ Fixed — 26 FDA, EMA, ICH and PMDA guidances
  now live on the [Resources](resources.qmd) page, each fetched and checked for
  draft-versus-final status. Two things worth knowing that came out of that
  sweep: **ICH M15**, the first harmonised MIDD framework, was finalised in June
  2026 and now sits above all the others; and FDA's 2020 *Clinical Drug
  Interaction Studies* guidance no longer resolves on FDA's site, having been
  overtaken by **ICH M12** (final, August 2024).
- **No PDAC-specific pharmacometric modelling.** Strand `D`'s TGI→OS references
  are colorectal and renal cell carcinoma. A published tumour-growth-inhibition
  model fitted to pancreatic cancer data was searched for and not found in this
  pass; `D1-11` will have to say so, or the search has to go deeper.
- **Nothing on immunogenicity and anti-drug antibodies** beyond a mention inside
  the biologics reviews. `CASE-MAB` will need a source of its own.
- **Nothing on pharmacogenomics** — CYP2D6, CYP2C19, DPYD, TPMT — which `P-09`
  cannot honestly avoid.
- **Nothing on drug–drug interaction prediction**: static mechanistic models,
  the R-value approach, and when a DDI study is required rather than modelled.
- **Nothing on adverse drug reactions and safety pharmacology** apart from the
  cardiovascular tutorial in `S5–S6`.
- **Still no textbooks and no regulatory guidances**, for the reasons above.
